analysis.one_liner: Requires USDA to set and enforce pathogen-reduction limits for raw meat and poultry.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: after introduction in May 2003 it sat in House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress, despite 38 cosponsors including 5 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Agriculture Department to identify the pathogens that make people sick from meat and poultry, survey how contaminated raw meat actually is, set binding standards to reduce that contamination to the lowest level reasonably achievable with today's technology, and test plants for compliance. A plant that failed a standard and did not fix it could no longer label its products "inspected and passed." It would also have written into law the department's authority to enforce existing sanitation rules. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy and eat meat and poultry — essentially every household — would get raw products with lower levels of disease-causing bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli, since the department would have to set standards based on what the best-performing plants already achieve and test plants against them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who buys meat or poultry

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to publish a list of the pathogens that contribute most to foodborne disease from meat and poultry, within 60 days of enactment and updated annually [S3].

Requires statistically representative national surveys of how contaminated raw meat and poultry actually are, published in the Federal Register, so consumers and regulators know baseline contamination levels [S3].

Requires binding pathogen-reduction standards set at the lowest contamination level reasonably achievable with current technology, benchmarked against the best-performing quartile of plants, with a final standard for at least the first pathogens within about four years [S3].
Requires regular microbial testing of plants; a plant failing a standard that does not take corrective action may no longer label its meat or poultry as "inspected and passed" [S3].

Directs the Secretary to enforce existing HACCP and sanitation requirements in every official establishment, and clarifies that the Secretary has authority to issue and enforce pathogen performance standards, foreclosing legal challenges that the department lacks that authority [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors would bear the cost of microbial testing, sanitation upgrades, and process changes needed to meet the standards; some of that cost would likely show up in meat prices. Plants that could not meet the standards could lose the "inspected and passed" label, which is effectively their license to sell into retail channels.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for thousands of processing plants would partly pass through to consumers in the form of higher meat and poultry prices, hitting lower-income households hardest [S3].

The enforcement tool is limited: a non-complying plant cannot be labeled "inspected and passed," but the bill does not itself require recalls or plant closures, so a stubborn plant could keep shipping while the dispute is resolved [S3].

Setting binding contamination limits on raw meat and poultry is scientifically contentious, since consumers are expected to cook these products thoroughly; the bill acknowledges this by requiring a report on the feasibility of health-based standards before pushing further [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims to cut foodborne illness at its source, where contamination originates in slaughter and processing plants, by requiring standards that top-performing plants already meet — which suggests the burden falls mainly on the laggards. The main honest costs are testing and compliance spending, some of which reaches consumers as higher prices, and an enforcement mechanism that works through labeling rather than direct recall authority. On balance, a targeted public-health measure with real but modest economic costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce committees in May 2003, sent to subcommittees a few weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2005 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on May 22, 2003, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to both the Agriculture Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee [S3].
Within weeks it was sent to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it sat [S5].
The bill attracted 38 cosponsors — 33 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but no committee or floor action ever followed; the only further record is the sponsor's introductory remarks in March 2004 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors are better off: no mandatory pathogen standards, no regular microbial compliance testing, and no threat of losing the "inspected and passed" label ever took effect.

sides.party_line_note: Support leaned Democratic — 33 of 38 cosponsors were Democrats, with 5 Republicans — and no Republican ever brought the bill to the floor or through committee; opposition never appeared as a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would require regular microbial testing and binding pathogen-reduction standards benchmarked to the industry's best performers, and a failing plant could lose the "inspected and passed" label that lets it sell. Processors would carry compliance costs that partly pass through to consumers, while the benefit — lower contamination in raw meat and poultry — goes to the public. The industry's interest in avoiding these standards runs against the public's interest in safer food, and the bill's death without a vote left the status quo in place.

The bill would write into law the department's authority to set and enforce pathogen standards and to withhold the "inspected and passed" label, shielding its rules from legal challenges that it lacks that power. It strengthens, rather than restructures, the existing inspection regime.
